claims.text: Severe lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys produces substantial surface strain.
Surface strain governs HEA catalytic activity by changing metal–metal bonding and the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates.
Surface strain shifts the d-band center of the transition-metal atoms.
Optimizing intermediate binding energies through strain enhances reaction kinetics.
Increasing surface strain will optimize intermediate binding energies rather than moving them away from their optimum.
Increasing surface strain enhances long-term catalyst durability.
A conventionally synthesized HEA can provide a relatively low-strain baseline with a multimetallic disordered crystal structure.
Changing particle size can be used to engineer HEA strain.
Rapid cooling or altered annealing temperature can increase HEA lattice distortion and surface strain while preserving bulk composition.
Holding composition, electrolyte, temperature, pH, and morphology constant would help isolate strain from compositional and geometric effects.
Strain-induced changes in local electron density shift the d-band center.
Strain-adjusted binding of *OH, *H, or *O can lower kinetic barriers in oxygen- and hydrogen-evolution reactions.
Higher-strain HEAs will exhibit lower overpotentials than otherwise comparable lower-strain HEAs.
Higher-strain HEAs will exhibit steeper Tafel slopes, interpreted in the hypothesis as faster kinetics.
Higher-strain HEAs will exhibit higher current densities than the lower-strain baseline.
Higher-strain HEAs will be more stable during continuous electrochemical operation.
The proposed mechanism applies broadly to multielement transition-metal catalysts, especially HEAs, under electrochemical conditions.
The mechanism may not apply to binary alloys or monometallic systems because their configurational complexity and inherent lattice distortion are minimal.
The quantitative strain–performance relationship is not established and may depend on alloy composition and reaction environment.
A lack of statistically significant performance improvement, or worse performance, in the higher-strain group would falsify the proposed governing role of strain.
